analysis.one_liner: Funds the IRS to step up audits of high earners and big corporations.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2026 with 40 Democratic cosponsors, the bill sits in the House Appropriations Committee, which has taken no action since the referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill adds roughly $84 billion in IRS funding across fiscal years 2026 through 2031, aimed at auditing high-income individuals and large corporations, improving taxpayer services, and modernizing the agency's outdated technology. It also requires the IRS to report to Congress on a plan to shift enforcement toward wealthy taxpayers, and requires an independent Inspector General evaluation of that plan.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who rely on the IRS collecting the taxes that are already legally owed. When high earners and corporations underpay, everyone else either pays more or gets worse services. The bill funds more auditors focused on high incomes, better phone and filing assistance for regular filers, and a long-overdue overhaul of IRS computer systems.

how_it_helps.text: Appropriates $45.6 billion for IRS tax enforcement from FY2026 through FY2031, explicitly to determine and collect owed taxes, with funding rising from $3.6 billion to $12.2 billion per year [S3].

Appropriates an additional $9.6 billion for taxpayer services like pre-filing assistance, filing and account services, and taxpayer advocacy, plus about $28.5 billion for technology upgrades and business systems modernization to detect fraud and replace outdated systems [S3].

Requires the IRS to submit a biennial plan for shifting auditing and enforcement assets toward high-income individuals and large corporations, recruiting auditors with the skills to audit them, and to analyze how much of the gap between taxes owed and taxes collected comes from each income level [S2][S3].
Requires the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration to independently evaluate the IRS's plan and its progress, adding oversight of how the money is used [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury, which spends the appropriations; and high-income individuals and large corporations, who face a greater chance of audits that find taxes they legally owe. Any additional collected revenue goes to the Treasury rather than being earmarked by the bill itself.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Treasury; high earners and corporations audited

drawbacks.text: The bill adds spending without any offsetting budget cuts or revenue provisions in its own text: roughly $83.7 billion over six years across its four funding accounts [S3]. Supporters argue enforcement collections offset this; the bill itself does not guarantee that.

Expanding IRS capacity is a recurring political flashpoint, and skeptics of enforcement funding argue audit activity can spill onto filers well below the high-income targets the bill names; the bill addresses this only by writing the audit focus into required reports, not by statute [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: the government spends money up front to build an IRS capable of collecting taxes already owed by the highest-income filers, who have the resources to game complex rules. The main honest objection is fiscal uncertainty — the bill commits large appropriations and leaves it to reports and audits to show whether collections cover the cost. The reporting requirements are a strength, but the bill does not itself cap audits on ordinary filers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Appropriations Committee, which has taken no action on it; with the session running until January 3, 2027, it has never come up for a vote.

narrative.text: The Stop CHEATERS Act was introduced in the House on July 16, 2026 by Rep. Suzan DelBene [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Appropriations, which controls spending bills, and has had no further action [S5].
Forty House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans appear among the cosponsors [S4].

The bill specifies appropriations across four IRS accounts — enforcement, taxpayer services, operations support, and business systems modernization — totaling roughly $84 billion over six years, and requires recurring reports on enforcement focused on high earners and large corporations [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income individuals and large corporations benefit so far, because the enforcement effort aimed at them remains unfunded while the bill sits without action.

for.name: Suzan K. DelBene
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 40 cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-controlled Appropriations Committee has not acted on the bill [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill directs IRS auditing and enforcement resources specifically at these taxpayers and funds recruitment of auditors able to examine their returns. Their financial interest in avoiding that scrutiny runs against ordinary taxpayers who otherwise make up the shortfall.

industries.industry: Tax shelter and aggressive tax advisory services
industries.note: Services built around helping wealthy clients minimize or obscure tax liability face clients whose returns are more likely to be examined and challenged.

industries.industry: IRS technology contractors and systems vendors
industries.note: The bill appropriates roughly $25.4 billion for operations support and $3.1 billion for business systems modernization, creating demand for vendors who can replace the IRS's legacy technology. Taxpayers benefit from the same upgrades through faster, more accurate processing.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been referred to the House Appropriations Committee for over a portion of the final months of a session with no hearings, no markup, and no Republican cosponsors. Spending bills originate in that committee, and a stand-alone IRS funding bill with no bipartisan support has no realistic path to a floor vote before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027; unless the committee acts or language is attached to a larger appropriations package, it will die at the end of this Congress.
